theory.overview: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) process sequential data—text, speech, time series—where order matters. Unlike feedforward networks that process fixed-size inputs, RNNs maintain a hidden state that captures information from previous time steps. This memory allows them to model temporal dependencies: predicting the next word in a sentence, forecasting stock prices, or generating music. However, vanilla RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients in long sequences, leading to the development of more sophisticated variants like LSTM and GRU that can capture long-term dependencies.

sections.title: The Sequence Challenge
sections.content: Standard neural networks assume inputs are independent and fixed-size. But real-world sequences—sentences, audio, sensor readings—have variable length and temporal structure. The word 'bank' means different things depending on context ('river bank' vs 'bank account'). RNNs solve this by maintaining state across time steps.

sections.title: RNN Core Mechanism
sections.content: At each time step, an RNN combines the current input with the previous hidden state to produce a new hidden state and optionally an output. The same weights are used at every time step—parameter sharing across time!
sections.intuition: The hidden state $h_t$ is a summary of everything the network has seen up to time t. It gets updated each step, carrying forward relevant information.

sections.title: Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT)
sections.content: Training RNNs requires unrolling the network through time and applying backpropagation across all time steps. This is Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT). Gradients flow not just through layers, but through time steps.
process: Unroll network for T time steps
Compute loss at each step (or just final output)
Sum gradients across time for shared weights
sections.challenge: Gradients must flow through many matrix multiplications—can vanish or explode over long sequences

sections.title: The Vanishing Gradient Problem
sections.content: In vanilla RNNs with tanh activation, gradients are multiplied by weight matrices at each time step during backprop. Over many steps, gradients either shrink to near-zero (vanish) or explode to infinity. This makes learning long-term dependencies nearly impossible.
sections.demonstration: After T steps, gradient contains factor $W^T$. If eigenvalues of W < 1: vanishing. If > 1: exploding.
sections.example: Consider: 'The cat, which was sitting on the mat that was placed near the window overlooking the garden, ... was hungry.' The verb agreement ('was') depends on 'cat' from 15+ words ago. Vanilla RNNs can't capture this.

sections.title: LSTM: Long Short-Term Memory
sections.content: LSTMs solve the vanishing gradient problem through a clever gating mechanism. Instead of simple matrix multiplications, they use an explicit memory cell with gates that control information flow.

gates.name: Forget Gate
gates.purpose: Decide what to remove from cell state

gates.name: Input Gate
gates.purpose: Decide what new information to store

gates.name: Output Gate
gates.purpose: Decide what to output from cell state

sections.cellState: $C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t$—the memory highway that gradients flow through relatively unchanged
sections.intuition: The cell state is like a conveyor belt—information rides along it unchanged, only modified by gates when necessary. This allows gradients to flow across many time steps.

sections.title: GRU: Gated Recurrent Unit
sections.content: GRUs are a simpler alternative to LSTMs with fewer parameters but similar performance. They merge cell state and hidden state, using just two gates.
sections.simplification: Combines forget and input gates into an 'update gate', merges cell and hidden states
sections.comparison: GRU has 3 weight matrices vs LSTM's 4; often trains faster with similar results

sections.title: RNN Architectures by Task
sections.content: Different sequence problems require different RNN architectures.

architectures.name: Many-to-Many (synced)
architectures.structure: Input per step → Output per step

keyConcepts.name: Hidden State
keyConcepts.description: The memory vector that carries information across time steps.
keyConcepts.analogy: Like a person keeping notes while reading—summarizing what's been read so far

keyConcepts.name: Parameter Sharing
keyConcepts.description: Same weights applied at every time step—process variable-length sequences with fixed parameters.

keyConcepts.name: Unfolding
keyConcepts.description: Visualizing RNNs as a deep feedforward network by copying layers for each time step.

keyConcepts.name: Long-Term Dependencies
keyConcepts.description: Relationships between elements far apart in a sequence.
keyConcepts.challenge: Hard for vanilla RNNs, solved by LSTM/GRU gating

complexity.forwardPass: $O(T \cdot H^2)$ where T = sequence length, H = hidden size—matrix multiply per step
complexity.parameters: $O(H^2 + H \cdot D)$ where D = input dimension—hidden-to-hidden + input-to-hidden weights
complexity.lstmOverhead: 4× parameters of vanilla RNN (one set per gate)

steps.title: Initialize Hidden State
steps.description: Start with zero hidden state before processing sequence.

steps.title: Process First Input
steps.description: Combine input embedding with hidden state.

steps.title: Recurrent Update
steps.description: Hidden state now carries information from first word.

steps.title: LSTM: Forget Gate
steps.description: Decide what information to discard from cell state.

steps.title: LSTM: Input Gate
steps.description: Decide what new information to store.

steps.title: LSTM: Output Gate
steps.description: Decide what to output based on cell state.

steps.title: Final Prediction
steps.description: Use last hidden state (or all states) for output.

practiceProblems.title: Sequence Length Flexibility
practiceProblems.description: An RNN trained on sentences of length 10 can process sentences of length 20 at test time. Why?
practiceProblems.answer: RNNs share parameters across time steps—the same weights are applied at every position. The network architecture is independent of sequence length.
practiceProblems.explanation: Unlike feedforward networks with fixed input size, RNNs process one element at a time using recurrent connections. The hidden state carries all necessary context, regardless of how long the sequence is.
hints: Same weights at each time step

practiceProblems.title: LSTM Gate Count
practiceProblems.description: An LSTM with hidden size 128, input size 50. How many parameters?
practiceProblems.explanation: Each gate has weights: (hidden_size + input_size) → hidden_size, plus biases. 4 gates × (178 × 128 + 128) = 4 × 22,912 = 91,648 for weights + 512 for biases = 92,160. Compare to vanilla RNN: (128+50)×128 + 128 = 22,912 + 128 = 23,040.

practiceProblems.title: BPTT Gradient Flow
practiceProblems.description: In a vanilla RNN, gradient at time t must flow back through how many matrix multiplications to reach time t-10?
practiceProblems.explanation: Each time step involves multiplying by $W_{hh}^T$ during backprop. After 10 steps, the gradient contains $W^{10}$ as a factor. If the largest singular value of W is less than 1, this shrinks exponentially—vanishing gradients!
hints: Each step multiplies by weight matrix

practiceProblems.title: Forget Gate Behavior
practiceProblems.description: Processing a long document. At word t, the forget gate outputs [0.01, 0.99, 0.99, 0.01] for 4 cell dimensions. What does this mean?
practiceProblems.answer: Dimensions 2 and 3 remember almost everything (99% kept). Dimensions 1 and 4 forget almost everything (99% cleared), preparing for new information.
practiceProblems.explanation: Each cell dimension can behave differently. The forget gate gives fine-grained control over what to remember. This is why LSTMs can selectively remember/forget different types of information.

practiceProblems.title: Encoder-Decoder Architecture
practiceProblems.description: Design an RNN architecture for English to French translation using encoder-decoder.
practiceProblems.answer: Encoder RNN: processes English sentence → final hidden state becomes 'thought vector'. Decoder RNN: initialized with thought vector, generates French word by word. Use attention mechanism to focus on relevant encoder states during decoding.
practiceProblems.explanation: The bottleneck is the fixed-size thought vector—information compression. Attention fixes this by letting the decoder 'look back' at all encoder states. Without attention, long sentences suffer.

practiceProblems.title: Gradient Clipping
practiceProblems.description: Explain why and how gradient clipping helps RNN training.
practiceProblems.answer: When gradients explode (grow very large), weight updates become huge and training becomes unstable (NaN loss). Gradient clipping caps gradient norm: if $||g|| > threshold$, set $g = threshold \cdot g / ||g||$. This prevents explosions while preserving direction.
practiceProblems.explanation: Exploding gradients are common in RNNs with long sequences. Clipping is computationally cheap and effective. Typical threshold: 1-5. PyTorch: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_.

minigame.title: Sequence Predictor
minigame.description: Train RNNs to predict next elements in sequences. Watch hidden states evolve, compare vanilla RNN vs LSTM performance on long sequences, and visualize memory gates in action.
instructions: Choose a sequence task: character prediction, sine wave, or custom pattern
Select RNN type: Vanilla, LSTM, or GRU
Adjust hidden size and sequence length
Train and watch prediction accuracy over time
Visualize hidden state dynamics and LSTM gate activations

codeExample.code:
import numpy as np

class VanillaRNN:
    """
    Vanilla RNN implementation from scratch
    h_t = tanh(W_hh @ h_{t-1} + W_xh @ x_t + b)
    """
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, output_size):
        self.input_size = input_size
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.output_size = output_size
        
        # Xavier initialization
        self.W_xh = np.random.randn(hidden_size, input_size) * 0.01
        self.W_hh = np.random.randn(hidden_size, hidden_size) * 0.01
        self.W_hy = np.random.randn(output_size, hidden_size) * 0.01
        
        self.b_h = np.zeros(hidden_size)
        self.b_y = np.zeros(output_size)
        
    def forward(self, inputs, h_prev=None):
        """
        Forward pass through sequence
        inputs: shape (seq_len, input_size)
        Returns: outputs (seq_len, output_size), final hidden state
        """
        seq_len = inputs.shape[0]
        
        if h_prev is None:
            h_prev = np.zeros(self.hidden_size)
        
        # Store hidden states for backprop
        self.h_states = [h_prev]
        self.inputs = inputs
        outputs = []
        
        for t in range(seq_len):
            # Hidden state update
            h_t = np.tanh(self.W_xh @ inputs[t] + self.W_hh @ h_prev + self.b_h)
            
            # Output
            y_t = self.W_hy @ h_t + self.b_y
            
            outputs.append(y_t)
            h_prev = h_t
            self.h_states.append(h_t)
        
        return np.array(outputs), h_t

class LSTM:
    """
    LSTM implementation with forget, input, output gates
    """
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        self.input_size = input_size
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        
        # Combined weights for all gates
        # Concatenated: [W_f, W_i, W_C, W_o]
        self.W = np.random.randn(4 * hidden_size, input_size + hidden_size) * 0.01
        self.b = np.zeros(4 * hidden_size)
        
        # Forget gate bias initialization to 1 (remember by default)
        self.b[:hidden_size] = 1.0
    
    def forward(self, x_t, h_prev, c_prev):
        """
        Single LSTM step
        x_t: input at time t (input_size,)
        h_prev: previous hidden state (hidden_size,)
        c_prev: previous cell state (hidden_size,)
        """
        # Concatenate input and hidden state
        concat = np.concatenate([h_prev, x_t])
        
        # Compute all gate activations
        gates = self.W @ concat + self.b
        
        # Split into individual gates
        f = self._sigmoid(gates[:self.hidden_size])  # forget
        i = self._sigmoid(gates[self.hidden_size:2*self.hidden_size])  # input
        c_tilde = np.tanh(gates[2*self.hidden_size:3*self.hidden_size])  # candidate
        o = self._sigmoid(gates[3*self.hidden_size:])  # output
        
        # Update cell state
        c_t = f * c_prev + i * c_tilde
        
        # Update hidden state
        h_t = o * np.tanh(c_t)
        
        # Store for visualization
        self.gates = {'f': f, 'i': i, 'c_tilde': c_tilde, 'o': o}
        
        return h_t, c_t
    
    def _sigmoid(self, x):
        return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

class GRU:
    """
    Gated Recurrent Unit - simpler than LSTM
    """
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        self.input_size = input_size
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        
        # Weights for reset gate, update gate, and new gate
        self.W = np.random.randn(3 * hidden_size, input_size + hidden_size) * 0.01
        self.b = np.zeros(3 * hidden_size)
    
    def forward(self, x_t, h_prev):
        """Single GRU step"""
        concat = np.concatenate([h_prev, x_t])
        gates = self.W @ concat + self.b
        
        # Split
        z = self._sigmoid(gates[:self.hidden_size])  # update gate
        r = self._sigmoid(gates[self.hidden_size:2*self.hidden_size])  # reset gate
        h_tilde = np.tanh(gates[2*self.hidden_size:])  # candidate
        
        # Update hidden state
        h_t = (1 - z) * h_prev + z * h_tilde
        
        return h_t
    
    def _sigmoid(self, x):
        return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

def gradient_clip(grads, max_norm=5.0):
    """Clip gradients to prevent exploding gradients"""
    total_norm = np.sqrt(sum(np.sum(g**2) for g in grads))
    clip_coef = max_norm / (total_norm + 1e-6)
    if clip_coef < 1:
        return [g * clip_coef for g in grads]
    return grads

# Demonstration
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== RNN Comparison Demo ===")
    
    # Problem: Predict next number in sequence
    # Training data: [0, 0.1, 0.2, ..., 1.0] → predict next value
    
    seq = np.linspace(0, 1, 20)
    X = seq[:-1].reshape(-1, 1)  # inputs
    y = seq[1:].reshape(-1, 1)   # targets
    
    # Vanilla RNN
    print("\n1. Vanilla RNN:")
    rnn = VanillaRNN(input_size=1, hidden_size=16, output_size=1)
    outputs, _ = rnn.forward(X)
    mse = np.mean((outputs - y)**2)
    print(f"   Untrained MSE: {mse:.4f}")
    
    # LSTM
    print("\n2. LSTM (single forward pass):")
    lstm = LSTM(input_size=1, hidden_size=16)
    h = np.zeros(16)
    c = np.zeros(16)
    lstm_outputs = []
    for x_t in X:
        h, c = lstm.forward(x_t.flatten(), h, c)
        lstm_outputs.append(h[0])  # Just using first dimension as 'output'
    
    print(f"   Forget gate (first step): {lstm.gates['f'][:5]}")
    print(f"   Input gate (first step): {lstm.gates['i'][:5]}")
    print(f"   Cell state range: [{c.min():.3f}, {c.max():.3f}]")
    
    # GRU
    print("\n3. GRU:")
    gru = GRU(input_size=1, hidden_size=16)
    h = np.zeros(16)
    for i, x_t in enumerate(X[:3]):
        h = gru.forward(x_t.flatten(), h)
        print(f"   Step {i}: h mean={h.mean():.3f}, std={h.std():.3f}")
    
    print("\n=== Key Differences ===")
    print("Vanilla RNN: Simple, suffers from vanishing gradients")
    print("LSTM: 4 gates, explicit cell state, best for long sequences")
    print("GRU: 2 gates, merged cell/hidden, faster, often comparable performance")
    print(f"\nParameters: RNN ~ {16*16 + 16*1 + 16:,}, LSTM ~ {4*(16+1)*16 + 4*16:,}, GRU ~ {3*(16+1)*16 + 3*16:,}")
